utterances.text: If we could call up P2708 which is the trial transcript, if we could go to page 5, the bottom paragraph in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: In this paragraph in the trial transcript this is what you stated according to this transcript, which you already said is not entirely complete. But it is recorded there the same way that you just explained it today, that it was the very day the brawl occurred that Nesic had threatened you once more in the morning. And I don't want to go through the transcript I just want to point out --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And I wish to tender the transcript in whole, Your Honours, at this stage, because we have looked at so parts and I think it is necessary for you to have the whole document and this fact is actually confirmed by the injured party in this transcript, which is on page 14 of the English version and it is also confirmed by another witness, Blagojevic, on page 18 of this very transcript that Mr. Dorovic had, indeed, been threatened by Mr. Nesic that very morning of that particular day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In tendering this whole transcript, though, for us to consider, is it to assist determination of this point or are you saying that the whole content should be considered for their own merits?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I'm tendering it for this particular point, Your Honours, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Because I got the impression that the witness doesn't accept all of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. He says it's incomplete, and against this background the argument would be that even though it is incomplete that this transcript, even under this premise confirms what he said was the context in which this incident occurred. And I would now like to ask some more questions about the incident as he would describe it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the situation as you've presented it, is no different from the situation in relation to any other exhibit that we've considered. We will take account of it insofar as it appears to us to cast light on other evidence and to be of value in itself, and we will do that in the light of the comments made about it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic, I would like you -- there was some talk about a pistol being involved in this incident and I would like you to explain as short and precise as you can what was the situation with regard to this pistol.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This pistol, I took it away during the brawl and this was the pistol of Dragoljub Zdravkovic, as was later established. This pistol, I handed over to Cvijic. Witnesses say that he was here on the premises, that is, during the brawl. You have the statement of witness Zdravkovic, who is the current prosecutor, then of witness Blagojevic, who also confirms that Cvijic as the security organ was there all the time on the premises. On the morning the next day I gave Cvijic that pistol and there is a certificate to that effect. I asked for him to carry out his expertise, and there is a certificate in writing on his behalf as security organ that this pistol was handed over. It's not my pistol. It is the pistol that I at one point in time during this clash took away from Zdravkovic and it ultimately turned out that it was a police pistol --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Dorovic --

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I just wish to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dorovic. Can you tell me whether you normally kept a pistol of your own.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that moment I did not have a pistol. Just the day before that on the 29th in the evening, on advice from my commander, Colonel Pesic, I was issued with an automatic rifle. And he advised me to sleep in the office. As a matter of fact, he asked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was there ever an occasion in 1998 or 1999 when you kept a pistol?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I had my own service pistol. I do have a pistol service. All officers have service pistols --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- but then I got a rifle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, the rifle's of no concern to anything that's arisen in the case so far. Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Sir, why did you take this pistol away from Mr. Zdravkovic in the situation?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because we exchanged a few blows. I used to be a successful sportsman. I did karate. I was a strong man. I managed to defeat him. He was a stronger man than I was, and that's why he thought that he could handle me and humiliate me. But as we were fighting at one moment, I managed to take away his pistol; and at one point in time, the police appeared. It was Corac precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes. And when you took the pistol away from Zdravkovic, where was it?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This happened in my office.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: So when Corac and the others entered the office, you had the pistol in your hand. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and I never pointed it at the police, never ever would I have done something like that. I'm a prosecutor. I had never seen that man in my life. I actually do not even know whether he was there. This Corac, actually. I first saw him at the trial in Nis. From the commander -- [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic, for the first time I think in this trial, I've used the button here to silence the microphone of someone who is not doing as the Court requires him to do. You were asked a simple question which you answered, and there was no need to give us the rest of your life's history in addition. Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: After Corac and the others had arrived and you had the pistol in your hand, when did you give the pistol? When did you turn it over? And please, really, focus on this exact a question. We go through step by step.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The following day when Cvijovic, the security organ, came to see me. I told him what it was that had happened, and I gave him the pistol. He wrote a certificate stating that I had handed over the pistol.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And that particular day, the 30th, after what had happened in the morning, once more how did you feel that day in terms of your personal security?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, if people who kill and who you know killed tell you that they will kill you, if they insult you, if they threaten you, like Nesic did to me in front of 60 people. He told me that he did not need that kind of prosecutor, that he would liquidate me or expel me. And he was swearing on me at ethnic grounds. He cursed my Montenegrin mother. For me, that is a terrible insult. So it was more of that than fear. At that moment I could not think about the actual impact of everything he had said to me. The only thing that was in my head was that this was a man who was powerful and dangerous, and particularly because he asked me not to mention, not to say, not to think about doing anything about Stosic. And I knew that he was an exceptionally dangerous man, the most dangerous man in the army, and I as the prosecutor knew about him, had occasion to know about him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So on the other hand if somebody publicly --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your microphone's been silenced again; and if this happens again, then we will bring your evidence to an end. You will not get a chance to clarify the things that the Prosecutor wishes you to have a chance to clarify after cross-examination if I have to do this one more time. Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Can we call up Exhibit P2731, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: As we discussed earlier today, the first-instance court issued an order for a neuropsychiatric examination of you, and was this decision overturned to your knowledge at some point? And just a yes or no would suffice.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And if you look at the document that is on the screen, do you recognise this decision as a decision -- as the very decision which overturned the decision of the first-instance court?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's it. That is that decision of the supreme military court.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And can we go to page 3 in the English version, please. Yes, go down a little, please, further.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: This decision states that this so-called expert was never in any personal contact with you nor was he present at the trial session as such. Can you confirm that, because you were there?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. That's what I assert. I don't even know the man --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I've never seen him in my life.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now, can we call up Exhibit P2759, please, the last page in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: You -- it was discussed with you earlier that the judge in the first-instance trial was Judge Popovic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first it was Radenko Miladinovic who --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, you've said that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've had that whole story from you. You've been asked a simple question if the judge that actually dealt with the case was Judge Popovic, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, these were proceedings going on for eight years. If we're talking about the moment of expertise, yes, it was Popovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Moeller --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before that --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: That's all I needed to know, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I don't see the exhibit on the screen yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: This is another request for assistance that we, the Office of the Prosecutor, sent to Serbia and Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Can we have the English exhibit? Okay. The request for assistance was addressed to Serbia requesting files on the proceedings we discussed earlier today against the three persons against which the proceedings were then ended, as we heard today. And on page -- on the last page, if we could go there, if we could zoom in. Yes. That was sent on 30 November 2006 and there is mentioned that there is an ongoing criminal procedure number VP Ki 1738/05 against Vukadin Milojevic and Zoran Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Is this the very proceeding you mentioned when you talked with Mr. Cepic about whether or not there are still proceedings ongoing against persons who triggered the proceedings against you?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and they forged records --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and one of the incriminations in --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. And this Zoran Popovic is the very Judge Popovic that we were just talking about?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I see Mr. Cepic on his feet, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise for interrupting the examination of my learned friend Ms. Moeller; however, it seems to me that there is an omission. On page 51 in line 9 my colleague said "expert" when she was commenting document P2731. She said "alleged expert"; however, in the document it doesn't say "alleged expert." It says "expert." That's the only mistake that was made. I believe it's an important one, and I believe that it was inadvertent on the part of my colleague in terms of interpreting the words that are there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your comments are noted, Mr. Cepic. Please continue, Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Moving away now from this subject and moving on to some other issues that were discussed during yesterday and today, today several documents were shown to you and yesterday also there was mentioning of a mass grave at Pusto Selo. The mass grave near Orahovac that you talk about in your statement in paragraph 35, has that anything to do with this mass grave at Pusto Selo that you were asked questions about, to your knowledge? And yes or no would, again, suffice.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say neither yes or no, because I don't know the exact location in view of the name of this place, that is. I assume -- but I'm not sure of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You assume what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That it could be linked up if it has to do with the same place --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now going back to something Mr. Visnjic asked you yesterday about particular requests that you sent to the authorities requesting that the disciplinary proceedings regarding the Natasa Kandic event be ended against you, and Mr. Visnjic showed Exhibit 2735, which we don't have to call up again. My question is only: How many of such requests did you send since this proceeding was initiated to official authorities?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to be precise. Proceedings are considered initiated on the day when the decision is brought on carrying out a disciplinary investigation --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic, please, let us try to focus on what I want to adduce from you. Please listen for a second. How many times did you request that these proceedings be ended one way or another? Just give us a number or -- if you can.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, now I understand what you are saying. Many times. Unfortunately, I cannot say, but really, many times. I requested the minister through the head of department, through the military court in Belgrade, and indeed that court did call upon the ministry to have a decision made with respect to this matter. I even had to write an open letter in the press --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I cannot give you the exact number so --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay, okay -- okay --

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- ten times.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, there was also an issue about how many times you actually requested to be released from your position as the military prosecutor. And my learned friend Mr. Visnjic tendered two exhibits in this regard yesterday. And you said yesterday in response that there were other requests that weren't tendered.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Can we call up Exhibit P2753, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Is that already the Serbian version? I don't think so. Now it's on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Could you look at that. Is that another request you sent on 1st June 1999 to be released of your position?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the fourth time in my career as a prosecutor, I believe that earlier today to Mr. Cepic's question I clearly said that this was on the 1st of June, and yes, this is the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now, can we call up Exhibit 2712, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Which is the official note that was made by Mr. Karan on the talks he had with you about a number of aspects and complaints that you made, which was discussed extensively yesterday with Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Can we go to the point 4 of this document. I think it's page 3 -- sorry, page 4. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic pointed out yesterday things that he did not find in this official note. If you look at point 4, Mr. Karan notes that you discussed with him the issue, the allegations that evidence was destroyed about some crimes. Can you confirm that you raised this issue with him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just one moment. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that if a question is put, the paragraph should be read through, because what this point 4 refers to and if we are looking at the same thing - I don't know what you have before you - has nothing whatever to do with what I asked the witness about and what witness talked in response to my question. I questioned the witness about the period relevant to the indictment, whereas here under bullet point 4 a reference is made to an entirely different development and this does not arise from my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think anything in a document that has been explored in cross-examination that might help explain the witness's answers is plainly something that may be raised in re-examination; yet the outcome of the examination is a matter for comment in due course. And you can continue with the question, Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: As I said, this note refers to one bullet point: "Evidence was destroyed ..." Did you discuss these allegations with Mr. Karan in this meeting?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the entire day, around 8.00, about serious things mostly --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- later on --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. And if you look at the end of the paragraph above that, there is also mentioning of a case against Milovan Tijanic. Did you also discuss this Tijanic matter with Mr. Karan in this meeting?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could my learned friend tell me where a reference is made to Tijanic, where his name is mentioned --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we have a B/C/S version which is completely --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: At the end of paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yeah, it's visible now but in my copy it was -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. No need to apologise. Can you now answer the question, please, Mr. Dorovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I spoke about Tijanic. I spoke about more than a hundred cases. I primarily insisted and I'm grateful for having been given occasion to speak about what they had done --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the people from the security services, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that there were grounds for my remark. Could the Prosecutor read to the witness the entire part that is illegible here save for the name of the witness. Maybe the Prosecutor could read to the witness what is the case involved, before what court, and against whom. Maybe the Prosecutor should read all that to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: If we could have the English version back on the screen I can do that, certainly. And the relevant text is: "... And a case against Milovan Tijanic conducted by the military court in Nis." I would --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you waiting for my comment? I spoke about the proceedings against Tijanic which were conducted before the war court affiliated with the command in Belgrade, but I know that Tijanic was also processed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on. Mr. Aleksic, what's the problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During this witness's examination-in-chief no reference was made to the proceedings in Nis. I agree that we spoke about the proceedings in Belgrade, but now we're talking about these proceedings in Nis. The name Tijanic and the case before this witness as a prosecutor in Belgrade, yes, but the case in Nis, this is something new.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a case by the security organs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please don't speak until I invite you to. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Anything else you want to say, Mr. Aleksic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, nothing else. This is the first time we hear of the case against Milovan Tijanic before the court in Nis. The witness never mentioned this, either on his direct or on the cross, and I don't think it should be allowed to him to now start talking about this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Moeller, can you comment on that, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I only wanted to point out that this name appears in this document and I don't intend to lead any further evidence -- or to ask any further questions on that. It was just a re-examination in relation to Mr. Visnjic's pointing out of what is all not contained in this document that I was pointing out that some things were indeed contained, some known names and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And no question arises of whether the witness discussed Tijanic in any other context that was referred to in cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Well, he said when I asked him earlier on, I think, that he discussed the case with Mr. Karan. I would need to check the transcript, but that's what I understood, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He was talking about proceedings before the war court affiliated with the command in Belgrade, and he also knows there were proceedings in Nis.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, so to me, that was answered the way that he discussed both matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic, regarding this incident with Mr. Tijanic, in the transcript of yesterday, page 11626 you said that what was done in this event was done on orders of Pavkovic and Ojdanic. In your statement you state that it was done on orders of Pavkovic and Lazarevic. Can you please clarify that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that the question is wrong. The witness did not say that it had been done on Pavkovic's and Ojdanic's orders. He said that Tijanic allegedly had the authority bestowed upon him from Pavkovic and Ojdanic. Please do not allow the Prosecutor to put questions in this way. He said that witnesses had told him that Tijanic had been given authority from Pavkovic and Lazarevic, and yesterday he said that it was from Pavkovic and Ojdanic. This is the essence of his statement, both the written statement and his testimony yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you accept that, Ms. Moeller?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I accept that what the witness said in the statement is what he said, and if I misinterpreted that, then that was my mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I wasn't meaning to imply anything here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, please continue -- which paragraph in the statement is it, remind me?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: It is -- it's -- I'm sorry, Your Honours. I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I have it noted if I can find it, because --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. Paragraph 17 onwards which deals with -- and it's actually paragraph 17, the last -- the second-last sentence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, I have it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: So, sir, my question was: In the statement you said that from the written statements it occurred -- or the written statements contained that these operations carried out by Tijanic were done on orders of Pavkovic and Lazarevic, and yesterday you said Pavkovic and Ojdanic. And I just wanted to clarify this point, please, and shortly if you can.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tijanic himself claimed that he did everything on the order of Pavkovic and Lazarevic. The witnesses, on the other hand, who were supposed to either contest or confirm his testimony also said that they had provided assistance. Those were witnesses that provided material goods, and they had certificates to that effect. We asked them to tell us whether they had provided that material and if they indeed did, what was the purpose of providing those things, because we're talking about a lot. And each and every one of them told the security organs, and I subsequently read these statements, they all claimed that they provided assistance to Tijanic in order to help the army, the Pristina Corps, and our units on Kosovo. This is what they claimed. Yesterday, to Mr. Visnjic's question, I said that I thought that this was done pursuant to an order. Furthermore, if you will allow me, I can also clarify this. Tijanic at that time in Belgrade pursuant to that criminal report and in those proceedings was also answerable for such a collection of things in Kosovo. At that moment the security organs insisted on the abuse of official position that he was also involved in when he was in Kosovo. A reference was made to a car company from Pristina to several repair companies, and later on it turned out that all that was true and this was also discussed both in Belgrade and --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm still not clear. Why and in which role, if any, did you mention General Ojdanic yesterday in this context?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tijanic claimed that he had permissions by the minister of defence, the Chief of the General Staff, and everybody in the state and that whatever he was doing, he was doing it continuously in Serbia, in the entire territory of Serbia where he collected assistance and help --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- he also claimed that he was doing that with the permission of Minister Pavle Bulatovic, General Ojdanic, and he mentioned all the other generals as well. He literally claimed that he was doing everything pursuant to order starting with minister across the entire military leadership and that this was his task, the task he was entrusted with to carry out.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that clarifies this issue. My last --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm glad you've got it clear. What we have is the minister and the whole senior army officers --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- now, which is rather different from yesterday's answer and rather different from the answer in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Maybe one follow-up question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Who ever mentioned or implied General Ojdanic in this to you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that this question should be ruled out. It's not admissible. Bearing in mind the fact that the witness has provided three answers. She has had three opportunities to ask this question. This is very much a leading question, and this is my chief objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: None of these objections are well-founded. It's a perfectly appropriate question for re-examination. Please continue, Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Sir, the question was: Whoever mentioned or implied General Ojdanic in these events to you? And please be short.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already told you, it was Tijanic. Tijanic claimed that he was doing that with the permission of the state leadership, the military leadership, and then he named people who had allegedly allowed that. When he was naming them he said everybody from the minister of defence to General Lazarevic and he also mentioned General Ojdanic among all these names. This is what he said, and you can see it in his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the last aspect I need to address with you is the disappearance of these 17 case files that we talked about yesterday, paragraph 27 of your statement. And I want you to be very short and specific in your answers, because I will be very specific in my questions. These cases were first with you; correct? Yes or no suffices.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were first my cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And then, according to paragraph 27 of your statement, they were turned over to Spasojevic, meaning the military prosecutor at the Pristina command; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And at the time they were turned over from you to him, where these files complete, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And why not?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some important documents were missing, some important evidence was missing from them, from those case files.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And how did this come about?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Somebody just removed the documents that are mentioned in the request to conduct investigation and in the request to carry out certain investigative procedures.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And when did that happen?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I filed my report, convinced that this had happened on the 29th of May and on the 30th of May. And I blame the security organs, Nesic, Cvijovic, and others for that very openly. I was very suspicious of them, and I also filed a report against the president of the court as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So how did -- how did these papers disappear while the files were in your custody?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Somebody simply removed them. Not the entire case files went missing, just some documents from those case files. 15 investigations were ongoing at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that happened while these files were in your office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They could not have been in my office, Your Honours. They could have been in the office of the court and the investigative judges --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- those were cases pending trial. I am a prosecutor, Your Honours, and in our system at one point in time everything is turned over to the court and while the court is in charge of the case, the case files are with the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: So these case files -- how did you know that documents had been removed from these files before they were turned over to Spasojevic?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the investigative judges asked us to state whether we adhered to our request for investigation, i.e., request for certain investigative procedures. Since the court declared itself territorially incompetent and in that case I as a prosecutor, together with my deputies, had to inspect every single case file in order to state our view. After we had read the requests, either for the investigations or for some investigative procedures, we saw it very clearly that in the description of the criminal act certain documents were mentioned, certain certificate on confiscated goods. Some official notes and other things which we could not locate in the case files. In order for us to be able to decide, I ran up to the president of the court, and from him requested to complete the case files. And then he told me, Dorovic, forget everything. This has already been decided. Another person will be in charge of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. So I understand - and tell me if I correctly understand - these files were not turned over from your prosecutor's office but actually from the court, that you reviewed them before they were turned over?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I registered every case, and in every case file there is my request --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please stop. The question is about which office they actually left last before going into the hands of Spasojevic. Was it from you or from the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the court's office. That was the final place where they were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And you say at this stage documents within the files were missing; correct?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what I was able to observe, together with my deputies, at the time, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And then -- the rest of the files were turned over to Spasojevic?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, to his court, because he was a prosecutor. This case involving the grave was turned over to him personally. As for the rest, they were referred to the court with the command of the Pristina Corps with a reference to the KV number.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. Now I think that clarifies it to some extent. What happened then to these files, if anything, after they were turned over to the court at the Pristina command?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you that. Spasojevic just consulted me about the mass grave case and told me that it had been decided that he would proceed in this case. What happened to these cases, what the final decision was, I really don't know, what happened to these cases. What happened to them, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think that clarifies paragraph 27 in the statement which is in its form not clear. And I think that also concludes my re-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Moeller. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have nothing special to say in relation to the examination we heard just now, the re-direct. However, I would just like to draw your attention to something. Since my colleague asked for all of 2D708 to be -- P2708 to be exhibited and I did not speak about that but 3D543, Cvijic's statement, I would like the Court to look at that in its entirety, too, in relation to the entirety of document P2708.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you have anything to say on that, Ms. Moeller?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand documents in cross-examination to go in to the record as far as the witness responds to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And that would be our position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But that extends to those aspects of the document that need to be considered to put everything that's been said by the witness in context. And on the face of it, this document looks as though it falls into that category. The problem I think may arise in the Defence case because there may be an issue over the reliability of that document. All we would be concerned about at the moment would be its prima facie value I think, and if it's a question of looking at the overall context, then we would regard any part of that document that we needed to have regard to for that purpose. But it will not be a document that's admitted like a statement might be admitted in the presentation of a party's case. If Mr. Visnjic wants to establish that positively as a piece of his evidence beyond the point that's it's been confirmed by the witness, then he will have to do that as part of the Defence case. But for the moment we will look at it in the context in which it was presented to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: -- say one more thing. That's my concern, because Mr. Visnjic referred Your Honours in his cross-examination to a high number of statements, and it's our understanding he cannot just tender statements of witnesses in full in cross-examination without calling this witness, bypassing Rule 92 and other rules that allow witness evidence to go in. That's why I made this request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But any document will be considered by us to assist in setting the evidence that the witness has given in context, and we will obviously need to look at documents which have been quoted in -- by Defence counsel in putting questions. And if reading more of the document's necessary to understand exactly what the question was getting at, then we'll need to read it. But beyond that, I don't go. If the statement is to be regarded by us as a statement that was actually made by the witness, then that will have to be proved as part of the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps we are now in a situation that we haven't had before. I did not cross-examine the witness about some things that Mr. Aleksic and Mr. Cepic examined him about. Later on Ms. Moeller availed herself of the opportunity provided by her re-direct, and I think that from that point of view the witness said something on the basis of which perhaps I could ask for additional examination, but I would like to avoid additional examination, and that is why I just wanted to draw your attention to this document which was already there in the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we are speaking theoretically now. I don't think this document is really important, but what happens if from somebody else's cross-examination something crops up which may give me the right to put some additional questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You can apply to cross-examine further if those following you raise issues which could be held against you, because you have a right to answer anything that's said against you. But I think you've identified a very practical way of dealing with the situation here with, which is to invite us to look at the document in the context of the re-examination as well as in the context of your cross-examination. And we're content to do that, but we do -- you will appreciate that any documents that the Defence use may yet be challenged by the Prosecution as unauthentic until they're proved at a later stage. There may be some that actually are proved in the course of the Prosecution case, but the majority will have to be established in your own case. You've actually identified a problem which will arise at a later stage in this case when we get to the Defence case and Defence counsel are cross-examining another Defence counsel's witness, then the sort of situation you envisage where things might be said against you later could well arise, and we'll just have to deal with any application you made to avoid injustice. That's a common problem in this sort of adversarial process. We'll deal with it according to the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic, that completes your evidence here -- oh, I'm sorry, maybe it doesn't complete your evidence. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I would like to deal with some different issue. Actually, my learned friend, Ms. Moeller, mentioned about Exhibit P2708 that would be useful to tender just parts of this evidence, but I do have completely opposite opinion because that is an exhibit which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, she asked the opposite. She asked the Court to take account of --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: The whole -- okay. I had completely different -- excellent. We completely agree about it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that does bring your evidence to an end, Mr. Dorovic. Thank you very much for coming to the Tribunal to give evidence. Whatever we make of it at the end of the day this has been an extremely helpful episode in the trial. Your evidence has come to an end and you're free to leave. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask for the possibility to say one sentence, please, Your Honour? Briefly? A brief sentence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you capable of that? Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we'll see. It is a unique opportunity for me to thank General Ojdanic for not having signed the draft submitted to him by General Gojovic. Had he done that, I and my family would have been destroyed, but he's the one who created General Gojovic, and he knows that full well. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Dorovic. You're now free to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's next, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have no further witnesses today. We have a videolink scheduled for tomorrow. The witness that is scheduled for Friday I'll have to advise you about later. He was supposed to travel today, but I'm not informed yet as to whether or not he's arrived. We will let you know as soon as we have any information about K87.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We need to make special effort to complete a videolink in one day, and that may need tailoring any proposals you have at the moment since we only have I think the basic four hours tomorrow, unless something changes between now and then. But on the schedule at the moment we only have the basic period. On the other hand, we could have got more time for you on Friday if you had wanted, but -- so you should keep working. I don't think -- I should have raised with Ms. Moeller there the question of exhibits. I don't think there are any issues arising in relation to the exhibits from the last witness, because you made your position clear insofar as you didn't refer to them. If you wanted them exhibited you, would have to tender them in a different way. And so your position is confined to the admission of those that you referred to in the course of the examination of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's correct. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So there are no issues. I repeat what I said yesterday, though, about any exhibits that you seek to tender as part of the Defence case must be presented to us in an appropriate form no later than Friday. Just finally, Mr. Hannis, I raised a matter with you on Monday about Clark, General Clark, and we have outstanding a question of certification. I take it there's no advance on the information in relation to that matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, there is not, Your Honour. I -- while I'm up perhaps I can advise you of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We have the difficulty of interpreting the footnote in the -- in the response, and we still have that problem, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We have advanced beyond one point that I know. The Rule 70 provider was interested in seeing the decision concerning the other two which we now have. They are informed of that. But I think they were also awaiting a decision regarding a request for certification. As a practical matter, I think we're so near the end of time in our evidence that whatever the decision was, we probably are not going to be able to have General Clark here, not before the 23rd of March, even if we were able to resolve the pending matter regarding the US requested conditions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You surprise me, because you're not likely to have an overload next week, are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, it's not because of having too much court time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's availability?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's availability, yeah. And in connection with that, Your Honour, I should indicate to the Court, I e-mailed Mr. Dawson last night concerning - I don't know if you have been advised - concerning Mr. Burns. There is a personal matter that may make him unavailable next week. We're trying to see if there's any way we can resolve that but that may not work out. We do anticipate having Mr. Phillips here hopefully on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I hope you manage to resolve the problem of Friday's witness, and we shall resume tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 15th day of March, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.14 p.m.,
